# Less waste, more profit: a food-waste plan for Crumb & Co

## Summary

Crumb & Co throws away an estimated 12–15% of what it bakes, mostly bread and pastries left at closing time, plus smaller amounts of dairy and fruit that pass their dates in the back. That is money baked and then binned: at your current volumes, roughly £9,000–£11,000 a year in ingredients and labour. Bakeries that measure their waste carefully often cut it noticeably within a few months without selling less, because the measuring itself changes what gets ordered and baked. This report covers how to measure the waste, how to order and bake closer to demand, how to use what is left, who to donate to, and how to compost the rest, and ends with an action plan.

## 1. Measuring the waste now

You can't reduce what you don't measure, and a rough guess is usually wrong in a telling way: most owners underestimate pastry waste and overestimate bread waste.

**What to record.** For four weeks, at closing time, record every unsold item by product and count, and every ingredient thrown out in the back, by weight. A clipboard by the bin works; so does a shared spreadsheet on the shop tablet. Add a column for the reason: unsold, damaged, past its date, or a mistake in the bake.

**Who records it.** Whoever closes the shop, every day, without exception. It takes about five minutes. Make it part of the closing checklist rather than an extra job, and explain why it matters: the point is to bake the right amount, not to blame anyone.

**What to look for.** After four weeks, total the waste by product and by day of the week. Expect patterns like these:

- One or two products account for most of the waste. In many bakeries the top three products by waste make up over half of it.
- Waste is highest on particular days, often Mondays and the day after a bank holiday, when demand is lower but the bake stays the same.
- Some waste happens before anything is baked: cream and fruit ordered in bulk that goes off before it is used.

**Turn it into money.** Multiply each product's unsold count by its ingredient and labour cost (not its shop price). This tells you which waste costs you most, which isn't always the waste you see most of: a tray of unsold almond croissants can cost more than a whole rack of rolls.

Keep measuring after the first four weeks, in a lighter form: a weekly total per product is enough to see whether the changes below are working.

## 2. Ordering and forecasting

Most bakery waste is decided the day before, when the bake list is set. The aim is to bake closer to what will actually sell.

**Bake to the day, not the week.** Use your four weeks of records to set a different bake list for each day of the week. If Monday sells 30% less than Saturday, Monday's bake should be about 30% smaller. Review the lists every month and after any change in the area, like roadworks outside or a new office nearby.

**Watch the weather and the calendar.** Rain cuts walk-in trade; school holidays change the morning rush; a local event can double it. Keep a simple note in the bake book of what happened on unusual days, so next year's bake can learn from this year's.

**Bake in two waves.** Instead of baking everything before opening, bake about 70% of the expected bread first thing and a second, smaller batch late morning, once you can see how the day is going. This takes some reorganising of the morning shift, but it's the single change that cuts end-of-day waste the most in small bakeries.

**Accept some empty shelves at the end of the day.** Running out of a few items in the last hour is a sign of a well-judged bake, not a failure. Tell customers about it with a small sign ("We bake fresh every day and sell out: thanks for understanding") and offer pre-orders for anyone who needs a particular loaf.

**Order ingredients to match.** Order dairy and fruit twice a week in smaller amounts rather than once a week, and check dates on delivery. Your supplier will usually split a delivery for free if you ask. Store with "first in, first out" labels so older stock is used first.

**Take pre-orders.** Larger orders for offices, cafés and parties should be taken by noon the day before and added to the bake list on top of the usual amounts. Encourage regulars to pre-order their weekend loaf: it's guaranteed sales and better forecasting in one.

## 3. Using leftovers

Some unsold food is inevitable. The next best thing to selling it fresh is selling it as something else.

**Sell it off at the end of the day.** Reduce unsold items by half in the last 45 minutes, or join an app like Too Good To Go, where customers buy a "surprise bag" of end-of-day food for about a third of its price. Bakeries on these apps usually sell most of their bags, and the customers often come back at full price another day.

**Turn day-old bread into new products.** Day-old bread makes excellent breadcrumbs, croutons, bread pudding and bostock (almond-topped toasted brioche). These sell well, use ingredients you'd otherwise pay to bin, and can be made in quiet hours. Start with one product, price it to cover the extra labour, and see how it goes.

**Use trimmings and broken pieces.** Offcuts from cakes and broken biscuits can be sold as tasting boxes or used as toppings. Over-ripe fruit goes into muffins and compotes rather than the bin.

**Feed the staff.** Let staff take home anything still unsold after the sell-off and before donations are collected. It's a small perk that people appreciate, and it means nothing edible is thrown away.

## 4. Donating

Food that can't be sold can still feed people. Donating is good for the community and good for the shop's reputation, and it's straightforward as long as the food is safe to eat and you follow the usual food-safety rules.

**Local partners.** The obvious partners are the food bank at St Mary's, the night shelter on Station Road and the community fridge in the library, all within a mile. Apps like Olio connect businesses with volunteers who collect surplus food and share it locally, which suits small, irregular amounts.

**Make it routine.** Donations work when they're regular: agree a collection time with one partner (for example, every day at closing time for the night shelter) and a backup for days they can't come. Keep a log of what's donated; it's useful for your waste records and shows the community what you're doing.

**Food safety.** Donate only food that's within its use-by date and has been stored properly. Bread and pastries are low-risk; cream cakes and anything with fresh dairy need to be kept chilled and collected the same day.

## 5. Composting

What can't be sold, used or donated should be composted, not sent to landfill, where it produces methane.

**Food-waste collection.** Your waste contractor can provide a separate food-waste bin, typically collected weekly for about £8–£12 a week, and the food is turned into compost or biogas instead of going to landfill.

**Local growers.** Hollybank Community Garden, half a mile away, has said it would welcome coffee grounds and vegetable trimmings for its compost heaps. This costs nothing, and it's a good story for the shop.

**Keep it clean.** Compost bins must not contain plastic, foil or string. A clear sign above each bin saying what goes in saves a lot of sorting.

## 6. Staff and habits

None of this works unless the people baking and serving are on board, and in a team of six everyone's habits matter.

**Explain the why.** Share the four-week waste figures with the whole team, in money as well as in loaves. "We binned £850 of pastries last month" is more motivating than a percentage. Make it clear that the goal is to bake the right amount, not to catch anyone out: people hide waste when they think they'll be blamed for it.

**Give the bake list an owner.** One person, the head baker, should own the daily bake list and be allowed to change it. When everyone can add "a few extra, just in case", the extras add up to most of the waste.

**Make the closing routine easy.** A one-page closing checklist on the wall (reduce prices at 4:15, record waste at 5, pack donations, empty the food-waste bin) means the routine survives holidays and new staff. Laminate it; it will get flour on it.

**Talk about it weekly.** Five minutes at the Monday team meeting: last week's waste total, the best and worst product, and one idea to try. Small, regular attention works better than a big push once a year.

**Celebrate progress.** When the waste figure drops, say so, and consider sharing part of the saving with the team, such as a monthly staff breakfast paid for out of what you didn't throw away.

## 7. Tracking progress

Pick three numbers and look at them every week:

- **Waste as a share of what was baked**, by product. This is the main measure. Aim to bring the overall figure from around 13% to under 9% within six months.
- **Sell-out time** for your main breads. If you start selling out at 2 pm instead of 5 pm, the bake for that item is now too small; if you never sell out, it's probably too big.
- **Money recovered** from end-of-day sales, leftover products and the sell-off app, against what it costs in time.

A simple chart on the office wall, updated every Monday, is enough. If a number stops improving for a month, go back to the daily records for that product and look for the pattern.

## 8. Action plan

The five actions below will make the biggest difference for the least effort. Together they should cut waste by about a third within six months and save around £3,000–£4,000 a year.

| # | Action | Who | By when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Record all waste at closing time for four weeks, then weekly | Closing staff (Priya to set up the sheet) | Start Monday 2 November |
| 2 | Set a separate bake list for each day of the week from the records | Dan (head baker) | 30 November |
| 3 | Start the second, late-morning bake for bread | Dan and the morning shift | 14 December |
| 4 | Join Too Good To Go and halve prices on unsold items at 4:15 pm | Sophie (shop manager) | 9 November |
| 5 | Agree a daily closing-time collection with the Station Road night shelter, with St Mary's food bank as backup | Sophie | 16 November |

**Next steps after these five:** add one day-old-bread product (bostock is the easiest to start with), set up the food-waste bin with your contractor, and start the two-deliveries-a-week dairy order. Review progress at the Monday meeting each week, and look at the whole plan again at the end of January with three months of figures in hand.

# Welcome to Hollybank Community Garden

## Welcome, and how the garden runs

Thank you for joining us. Hollybank started in 2014 on a strip of council land behind the library that had been a car park, a dumping ground and, for one memorable summer, a home for a family of foxes. Today it is forty raised beds, a polytunnel, an orchard of eleven fruit trees, a pond and a shed that everyone agrees is too small. Around sixty volunteers keep it going, and none of us knew much about growing food when we started. You don't need to either.

The garden is run by a committee of six volunteers who are elected every March at the annual meeting. The committee looks after money, the lease with the council and the big decisions, like whether to build a second polytunnel (we are still arguing about that one). Day to day, the garden runs on three simple ideas. First, everything grown in the shared beds is shared: take what you need for your table, and leave enough for the next person. Second, we garden without chemical pesticides or weedkillers, so expect to do some weeding by hand and to make friends with ladybirds. Third, nobody has to do anything they don't enjoy. If you love watering and hate digging, water.

New volunteers spend their first two sessions with a buddy, an experienced volunteer who will show you around, introduce you to people and answer the questions you feel silly asking. There are no silly questions here. Several of us once spent a whole season carefully tending a row of what turned out to be dandelions.

## The weekly schedule

The garden gate is open whenever a volunteer with a key is on site, but most of the work happens in three regular sessions:

- **Tuesday evenings, 5:30 to 7:30 pm (April to September).** The watering and harvesting session. It's quieter, good for people who come straight from work, and the best time to pick salad leaves before they wilt in the sun.
- **Thursday mornings, 10 am to 12:30 pm (all year).** The heavier jobs: digging, building, turning the compost, pruning in winter. Tea and biscuits at 11.
- **Saturday mornings, 10 am to 1 pm (all year).** Our busiest session and the best one to start with. There's a short briefing at 10 at the shed, where the session lead writes the day's jobs on the whiteboard and you pick one. Families are welcome on Saturdays; children need to stay with an adult.

On the first Saturday of every month we stop at 12:30 for a shared lunch, cooked partly from whatever is ready in the beds. You don't have to bring anything, but if you like baking, you will be very popular.

You don't need to sign up for sessions, and nobody counts how often you come. If you'd like a regular job of your own, such as looking after the herb spiral or the pond, ask the session lead and we'll find you one.

## Tools and safety

The tools live in the shed, and the padlock code is changed every season and sent out in the volunteers' newsletter. Please put every tool back where you found it, cleaned of mud; there is a brush and a bucket by the door. Spades and forks hang on the left wall, hand tools are in the labelled crates, and the hose reels stay by the water butts.

A few rules keep everyone safe:

- **Wear closed shoes**, not sandals. Gloves are in the blue box by the door if you don't have your own.
- **Power tools** (the hedge trimmer and the strimmer) are only used by volunteers who have done the short training with Mike on a Thursday. Ask him if you'd like to learn.
- **Lift with your legs**, and ask for help with anything heavy, like compost bags or the water butt lids. Two people make light work.
- **Tetanus.** Garden soil can carry tetanus. If you aren't sure your jab is up to date, check with your GP before you start digging.
- **Cuts and scrapes** happen. The first aid kit is on the shelf above the sink, and there is a list of volunteers with first aid training pinned next to it. Wash any cut straight away and tell the session lead, who will note it in the accident book.
- **Children** must stay with their adult and away from the pond and the tool shed.
- **Hot days.** Drink plenty of water, wear a hat and take breaks in the shade of the orchard. The Tuesday session ends early if it's above 30 °C.

If something is broken, put it on the "needs fixing" shelf with a note rather than back on the wall.

## What to plant when

Our growing year follows the seasons, and the session lead will always tell you what needs doing, but it helps to know the rhythm:

- **March and April:** sow broad beans, peas, onions and early potatoes outside; start tomatoes, peppers and squash in the polytunnel. Weed the beds before the weeds win.
- **May:** plant out the tomatoes and courgettes once the frosts have passed (usually mid-May here). Sow beetroot, carrots and salad every two weeks for a steady supply.
- **June to August:** keep up with watering, tie in the tomatoes, pick everything often (picking courgettes small means more of them), and sow winter greens like kale and leeks.
- **September and October:** harvest the squash and the apples, plant garlic and onion sets for next summer, and sow green manure on empty beds to feed the soil.
- **November to February:** prune the fruit trees, mend paths and raised beds, spread compost, and plan next year over tea in the shed.

There's a planting chart on the shed door showing which bed holds what, and we rotate crops between beds each year so the soil stays healthy. If you're unsure whether something is a seedling or a weed, ask before you pull it.

## Who to ask for help

- **Your buddy** is your first port of call for your first few weeks.
- **The session lead** (their name is on the whiteboard) runs each session and decides the jobs.
- **Priya Shah** coordinates volunteers. Talk to her about anything from changing your sessions to feeling unsure about a task: priya@hollybankgarden.org.
- **Mike Doyle** looks after tools and power-tool training on Thursdays.
- **Jean Mburu** leads the polytunnel and knows more about tomatoes than anyone should.
- **Emergencies:** call 999 first, then the committee phone, 07700 900412, which a committee member always carries.

We're glad you're here. Come as often as you like, bring a friend, and don't worry about getting things wrong: the garden has survived all of us so far.

# budget.py

Monthly totals per spending category from your bank's CSV export.

## Setting up

1. Install Python 3.10 or newer, then the one extra package: `pip install pyyaml` (and `pip install pytest` to run the tests).
2. Export your transactions from your bank as CSV. Most banks call this "Download statement" or "Export". The file needs three columns: `date` (as 2026-09-14), `description` and `amount`, with money going out as negative numbers. If your bank names the columns differently, rename them in the first line of the file.
3. Copy `rules.yaml` next to the script and edit it (below).

## Writing rules

`rules.yaml` lists categories in order. Each has a name and keywords:

    categories:
      - name: Groceries
        keywords: [tesco, aldi, lidl]
      - name: Bills
        keywords: [octopus energy, council tax]

- A transaction goes to the **first** category with a keyword that appears anywhere in its description, ignoring capitals. Put specific keywords above general ones: `amazon prime` in Subscriptions above `amazon` in Shopping.
- Anything that matches no rule goes to **Other**. After each run, look at what landed in Other and add keywords for anything that recurs.
- Keywords can contain spaces. They match parts of words too, so `bp` would match "BP FUEL" but also "BPW LTD"; use a longer keyword if that happens.

## Running it every month

    python budget.py statement.csv --rules rules.yaml

prints every month in the file. To see one month, add `--month 2026-09`.

To run it automatically on the 1st of each month on a Mac or Linux, add a line like this with `crontab -e`, changing the paths:

    0 9 1 * * cd ~/budget && python3 budget.py latest.csv --rules rules.yaml > "summary-$(date +\%Y-\%m).txt"

That saves each month's summary as its own file. On Windows, Task Scheduler can run the same command.

## Tests

Run `pytest` in this folder. The tests make their own small CSV and rules files, so they never read your real statements.

# Backing up 400 GB of family photos: three options

Your photos are irreplaceable, and the most common ways to lose them are boring: a laptop dies, a phone goes in the sea, or a house is burgled. A good backup survives all of those. Below, three approaches are compared for a family with about 400 GB of photos that grows by roughly 50 GB a year. Prices are typical UK prices in 2026 and will vary.

## 1. An external hard drive

A 2 TB USB drive costs about £60–£70 and holds your whole library with plenty of room to grow. You plug it in and copy new photos across, ideally with backup software (Time Machine on a Mac, File History on Windows) so it happens automatically whenever the drive is connected.

- **Cost over five years:** about £65 for the drive, plus a replacement after four or five years for safety: £65–£130 in total.
- **Effort:** low to set up, but it depends on someone remembering to plug it in. In practice, many families' backups quietly stop in the second year.
- **Safety from fire or theft:** poor, if the drive lives next to the computer. A burglar takes both, and a fire destroys both. Keeping the drive at a relative's house helps, but then it is rarely up to date.

## 2. A cloud service

Services like iCloud, Google One or OneDrive store your photos on their servers and sync new ones automatically from phones and computers. For 400 GB growing to about 650 GB, you'll need a 2 TB plan, which costs around £8 a month.

- **Cost over five years:** about £480 (60 months at £8), more if prices rise.
- **Effort:** the lowest. Once it's switched on, every photo from every phone is backed up within minutes, with nothing to remember.
- **Safety from fire or theft:** excellent. The photos are in data centres far from your house, copied several times. The risks are different: losing access to the account (so set up two-factor authentication and recovery options carefully), and deleting photos by mistake, since a deletion syncs too (most services keep deleted items for 30 days).

## 3. A NAS at home

A NAS (network-attached storage) is a small box with two hard drives that sits on your home network. Photos from every device can back up to it automatically, and the two drives mirror each other, so one can fail without losing anything. A two-bay NAS with two 4 TB drives costs about £400.

- **Cost over five years:** about £400 up front, plus around £20 a year in electricity and probably one replacement drive (£90): roughly £590 in total.
- **Effort:** the highest to set up (an afternoon for someone comfortable with technology), then low, though someone needs to apply updates and notice warning emails.
- **Safety from fire or theft:** poor on its own, because it is in the house. Many NAS boxes can also copy themselves to a cloud service, which fixes this, at extra cost.

## At a glance

| | External drive | Cloud service | NAS at home |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost over 5 years | £65–£130 | about £480 | about £590 |
| Effort | Low, but easy to forget | Lowest: automatic | High to set up, then low |
| Safe from fire or theft | No (unless kept elsewhere) | Yes | No (unless it copies to the cloud) |
| Main risk | Nobody plugs it in | Losing the account | Same house as the originals |

## Recommendation

For most families, **use a cloud service as the main backup and an external drive as the second copy.** The cloud service runs itself and protects against fire and theft; the drive, refreshed every few months and kept at a grandparent's or a friend's house, protects against losing the cloud account or deleting something by mistake. Together that's about £550 over five years, and it follows the old "3-2-1" rule: three copies (the originals plus two backups), on two kinds of storage, with one away from home.

A NAS is worth it if you have a lot of video, several computers, or a family member who enjoys tinkering, but on its own it doesn't protect against the most serious risks, so you'd still want a copy outside the house.

# Learn the basics of SQL in 14 days

This plan assumes about 45 minutes a day and no programming experience. You'll use SQLite, which is free and needs no server: install **DB Browser for SQLite** (sqlitebrowser.org) on day 1 and you're set. Each day has a topic, something to read or watch, and a small exercise. The reading suggestions use two free resources throughout: the **SQLBolt** interactive lessons (sqlbolt.com) and the **SQLite tutorial** at sqlitetutorial.net, whose sample "chinook" music-shop database you'll download on day 1.

If you miss a day, just pick up where you left off. If an exercise takes longer than 45 minutes, stop and finish it the next day: understanding matters more than speed.

## Day 1: What a database is, and your first query

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lesson 1 (SELECT queries 101). On sqlitetutorial.net, read "Getting started" and download the chinook sample database.
- **Exercise:** Open chinook.db in DB Browser. In the Execute SQL tab run `SELECT * FROM artists;` and then `SELECT Name FROM artists;`. Write down how many artists there are (the count shows at the bottom).

## Day 2: Filtering rows with WHERE

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lessons 2 and 3 (queries with constraints).
- **Exercise:** Find all tracks shorter than two minutes (`Milliseconds < 120000`). Then find all customers from Brazil.

## Day 3: Sorting and limiting results

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lesson 4 (filtering and sorting query results).
- **Exercise:** List the ten longest tracks, longest first. Then list customers alphabetically by last name and show only the first five.

## Day 4: Text patterns and NULL

- **Read or watch:** sqlitetutorial.net: "SQLite LIKE" and "SQLite IS NULL".
- **Exercise:** Find every track whose name contains the word "love" (any capitalisation). Then find customers with no company (`Company IS NULL`) and count them.

## Day 5: Counting and summing

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lesson 10 (queries with aggregates, part 1).
- **Exercise:** How many invoices are there? What's the total of all invoices (`SUM(Total)`)? What's the average invoice total, rounded to two decimals?

## Day 6: Grouping with GROUP BY

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lesson 11 (queries with aggregates, part 2); sqlitetutorial.net "SQLite GROUP BY".
- **Exercise:** Count customers per country, biggest first. Then find the total sales per billing country from the invoices table.

## Day 7: Filtering groups with HAVING, and a review

- **Read or watch:** sqlitetutorial.net "SQLite HAVING". Re-read your notes from days 1 to 6.
- **Exercise:** List only the countries with more than five customers. Then write, in plain words, what each query you've written this week does.

## Day 8: Joining two tables

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lesson 6 (multi-table queries with JOINs). Watch a short video explaining JOINs with Venn diagrams (search "SQL joins explained").
- **Exercise:** Show each album's title next to its artist's name (join albums to artists on ArtistId). How many albums does Iron Maiden have?

## Day 9: LEFT JOIN and missing matches

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lesson 7 (OUTER JOINs).
- **Exercise:** Find artists who have no albums in the database, using a LEFT JOIN and `WHERE albums.AlbumId IS NULL`.

## Day 10: Joining more than two tables

- **Read or watch:** sqlitetutorial.net "SQLite INNER JOIN" (the three-table example).
- **Exercise:** List every track with its album title and artist name. Then find the five artists with the most tracks.

## Day 11: Creating your own table

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lessons 16 and 17 (creating tables, altering tables).
- **Exercise:** Create a new database file and a table `books` with columns id (integer primary key), title (text, not null), author (text) and year (integer).

## Day 12: Adding, changing and deleting rows

- **Read or watch:** SQLBolt lessons 13, 14 and 15 (inserting, updating, deleting rows).
- **Exercise:** Insert five books you like. Update one book's year. Delete one book. Run a SELECT after each change to see what happened.

## Day 13: Subqueries

- **Read or watch:** sqlitetutorial.net "SQLite Subquery".
- **Exercise:** In chinook, find the tracks that are longer than the average track length, using a subquery for the average.

## Day 14: Putting it together: a small project

- **Read or watch:** Skim your notes from all 13 days.
- **Exercise:** Answer three questions about chinook with your own queries: Which genre has the most tracks? Which customer has spent the most? Which month of 2010 had the highest sales? Save your queries in a text file: they're your first SQL portfolio.

## After the 14 days

You now know enough SQL to answer real questions about real data, which is most of what people use it for day to day. Good next steps: the free "SQL Murder Mystery" game (mystery.knightlab.com), window functions, and trying the same queries in PostgreSQL. Keep the habit of writing down, in plain words, what a query should return before you run it.
